clue.text: Hugs daughter twice, gripped by cryptic clues

indicators.note: something gripped is held inside whatever grips it, so one piece sits within the other
a cryptic arrangement is a puzzling, scrambled one, so these letters must be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange
D is the abbreviation for daughter, used two times

explanation.surface: A setter fondly hugs their daughter twice while puzzling over cryptic clues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cryptic clues' reads as the puzzle itself, but cryptic is the instruction to scramble the following word before the daughters go inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To hug someone is to embrace them warmly, and cuddles is the plural noun or verb form with that same sense.

clue.text: Conservative clubs are almost packed

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter of that word is dropped

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for clubs, the card suit
taken as written
a packed room is full

explanation.surface: Tory social clubs are said to be nearly full to bursting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conservative clubs' reads as a political phrase, but Conservative is the definition and clubs is just the card suit C.
explanation.definitionFit: A conservative estimate or approach is cautious and avoids risk, which is what careful describes.

clue.text: Quacks firstly from ducks observed crossing rocky hills

indicators.note: firstly points at the opening letter of each of the words that follow it

parts.note: the initial letters of these three words
a tor is a rocky hilltop, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: Someone notes the quacking of ducks seen waddling across rocky hills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quacks' seems to belong with the ducks, but it is the definition: quack is slang for a doctor. A tor is a craggy hill in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Quack is informal and slightly mocking slang for a medical practitioner, originally a fraudulent one.

clue.text: Ecstasy after John's free

indicators.note: after tells us the first-named piece is placed behind the next one

parts.note: john is slang for a toilet, as is loo
the possessive S taken as written
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: After taking ecstasy, John is free of his inhibitions.
explanation.walkthrough: John looks like a man's name but is slang for the toilet, the LOO; ecstasy the drug is E.
explanation.definitionFit: Something loose is not tied or held, so it is unconfined and at liberty.

clue.text: Rudely insist Eve is easily offended

indicators.note: doing something rudely means roughly and without order, so the letters are knocked about

parts.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: If you rudely insist on something, Eve takes offence easily.
explanation.walkthrough: The rudeness and the easy offence make a neat story, but 'Rudely' only tells you to rearrange the nine letters of INSIST EVE.
explanation.definitionFit: A sensitive person is quick to feel hurt by remarks, the same as being touchy or thin-skinned.

clue.text: Birds out of one's tree and beginning to sing

parts.note: out of one's tree means crazy, and so does cuckoo

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of this word

explanation.surface: Birds fly out of a tree and start to sing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of one's tree' reads as birds leaving a branch, but it is the idiom for crazy, which gives CUCKOO.
explanation.definitionFit: Cuckoos are a family of birds known for their two-note call and laying eggs in other nests.

clue.text: Tightly held bottom of electric organ

indicators.note: in a down entry the bottom of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the final letter of this word
the lung is an organ of the body

explanation.surface: Someone grips the base of an electric organ at a concert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Electric organ' sounds like one instrument; split it, taking the last letter of electric and reading organ as a body part.
explanation.definitionFit: Clung is the past tense of cling, meaning gripped on firmly and would not let go.

clue.text: Institutes protecting ancient city's animals

indicators.note: to protect is to surround and shield, so one piece wraps around the other

parts.note: to institute something is to establish or create it
Ur is the ancient Sumerian city of crosswords

explanation.surface: Learned institutes work to protect the animals of an ancient city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Institutes' reads as a noun for organisations but works as a verb meaning sets up; the 's stands for is.
explanation.definitionFit: Creatures is a general word for living beings, especially animals as distinct from people.

clue.text: Aida perhaps with little energy after tense run

indicators.note: after tells us the first-named piece is placed behind the next one

parts.note: Aida is an example of an opera, by Verdi
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense
little signals the abbreviation, E for energy

explanation.surface: A performer of Aida, low on energy after a tense run of shows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run' looks like a run of performances but is the verb meaning to manage; 'perhaps' marks Aida as an example of an opera.
explanation.definitionFit: To run a machine or business is to work or manage it, which operate also means.

clue.text: Incline to think American quietly is taken in by religious group

indicators.note: something taken in by another is absorbed inside it, so one piece goes within

parts.note: a sect is a religious group
US is the standard abbreviation for American
p (piano) is the musical direction for quietly

explanation.surface: One tends to think a quiet American has been drawn into a religious cult.
explanation.walkthrough: Quietly gives P because p, for piano, is the musical marking for soft playing.
explanation.definitionFit: To suspect something is to believe it likely without proof, a leaning towards thinking it true.

clue.text: Orca once nearly digested black-striped mammal

indicators.note: digested food is broken down and churned, so the letters are mixed up
nearly means not quite all, so the last letter of that word is dropped

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, before trimming

explanation.surface: A killer whale once very nearly ate a small striped animal.
explanation.walkthrough: The orca eating a mammal is a plausible picture, but 'digested' just says to rearrange ORCA plus ONC.
explanation.definitionFit: The raccoon is a North American mammal with black bands on its tail and a dark mask across its eyes.

clue.text: Rubbish fossil fuels recommendation?

definitions.meaning: second meaning, split in two: advice to burn smaller amounts of coal and oil

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a playful reading: split the answer into two words, USE LESS, and it is the advice environmentalists give about fossil fuels.
explanation.definitionFit: Something rubbish is worthless, and the split phrase is a familiar green slogan about consumption.

clue.text: Blooming depressed, cutting finger badly

indicators.note: a blade cutting something goes into it, so one piece is set inside the other
something done badly is botched and jumbled, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange
to feel depressed is to feel low

explanation.surface: Feeling bloody miserable after slicing a finger badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blooming' reads as a mild British swear word, like bloody, qualifying depressed; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plant that is blooming is in flower, producing blossoms, which is what flowering means.

clue.text: Drinks with English guy

parts.note: cups of tea are drinks
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Having drinks with an English bloke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Guy' looks like a noun for a man, but it is the British verb meaning to mock or make fun of someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To guy someone, in older British usage, is to ridicule or poke fun at them, the same as to tease.

clue.text: Someone who didn't win partly deplores Olympics, on reflection

indicators.note: a reflection in a mirror is back to front, so the letters are read the other way
partly means only a portion of the words that follow is used, a run of letters inside them

parts.note: these letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: An athlete who didn't win thinks back and condemns the Olympics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On reflection' reads as thinking it over, but here it means read backwards; RESOL spans deploRES OLympics.
explanation.definitionFit: A loser is literally the competitor beaten in a contest, the person who failed to come first.

clue.text: Resistance before training heartlessly is cut

indicators.note: without a heart means the central letter of that word is removed
before tells us the first-named piece comes in front of the next one

parts.note: R is the symbol for electrical resistance
training is a form of education

explanation.surface: A cruelly cut training budget meets resistance.
explanation.walkthrough: EDUCATION has nine letters, so its heart is the fifth, the A; dropping it leaves EDUCTION.
explanation.definitionFit: A cut in spending or price is a reduction, a lowering of the amount; both are nouns here.

clue.text: International rock concert including Queen? Wrong

indicators.note: including something means taking it in, so one piece goes inside
to rock is to shake to and fro, so the letters are shaken into a new order

parts.note: I is the abbreviation for international
taken as written
R stands for Regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: Was it wrong that the big international rock concert included Queen?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock concert' and Queen the band make a music scene, but rock is the anagram signal. All nine letters, I, CONCERT and R, are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Incorrect simply means not right or mistaken, a direct synonym of wrong as an adjective.

clue.text: Called for calm

definitions.meaning: first meaning: fetched someone, as from school

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a demand for calm, but 'called for' means picked up, as in calling for a friend at their house.
explanation.definitionFit: You collect someone when you fetch them, and a collected person is cool, composed and in control.

clue.text: Plant shoot in good condition

parts.note: to shoot along is to speed
to be in good condition is to be well

explanation.surface: A gardener notes that a plant's new shoot is healthy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shoot' fits the plant picture as new growth, but it is the verb meaning to race.
explanation.definitionFit: Speedwell is a small wild flower, usually blue, found in British hedgerows and lawns.

clue.text: Somewhere in Yorkshire, son takes up residence

parts.note: Settle is a market town in North Yorkshire
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A son moves to a place in Yorkshire and makes his home there.
explanation.walkthrough: Settle is a small market town in the Yorkshire Dales, in northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: To settle somewhere is to establish a permanent home there, moving in to live.

clue.text: Ruler, politician and monarch tucked into flipping caviar!

indicators.note: something tucked into another is pushed inside it, so one piece goes within
flipping something over turns it the other way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: caviar is sturgeon roe
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the late queen
an MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A ruler and his entourage gorging on blasted caviar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild British curse on the caviar, but it is the instruction to turn the fish eggs round.
explanation.definitionFit: An emperor is the sovereign ruler of an empire, a supreme head of state.

clue.text: Dismisses trousers lacking length

indicators.note: lacking something means being without it, so that letter is taken away

parts.note: slacks are casual trousers
L is the abbreviation for length

explanation.surface: A tailor gets rid of trousers that are too short in the leg.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the L out of SLACKS.
explanation.definitionFit: To sack an employee is informal for firing them, so sacks means dismisses from a job.

clue.text: Piece of fried food salesman picked up, full of beans

parts.note: a chip is a piece of fried potato

indicators.note: in a down entry, picking something up lifts it so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: a rep is a sales representative

explanation.surface: A travelling salesman picks up some fried food, beans included.
explanation.walkthrough: The fried food and beans paint a café breakfast, but 'full of beans' is an idiom for lively and is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Full of beans is an idiom for energetic and cheerful, and chipper means bright and lively.

clue.text: Moaned about tip on two-man saw

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: to sigh is to let out a moan or groan

indicators.note: the tip of a word is its very end, here its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter of this word

explanation.surface: Workers grumbled about the blade on a two-man saw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like the cutting tool of the surface, but it is the past tense of see.
explanation.definitionFit: To sight something is to catch sight of it, so sighted is a past-tense verb meaning saw.

clue.text: Sign of nerves about work issue

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: a nervous tic is an involuntary twitch
op is short for opus, a musical work

explanation.surface: A sign of nerves about a problem at work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Work issue' reads as one phrase about a job problem; split it, with work the musical OP and issue the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An issue under discussion is a subject or matter of debate, which is what a topic is.

clue.text: Bert returns holding minute fish, shaking

indicators.note: returning means going back the way you came, so the letters run backwards
holding something means keeping it within, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: taken as written
M is the abbreviation for minute
the ling is a sea fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: Bert comes back clutching a tiny fish, and he's shaking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minute' looks like the adjective for tiny describing the fish, but it is the time unit M.
explanation.definitionFit: Trembling and shaking both describe quivering involuntarily, from fear, cold or excitement.

clue.text: Augusta's tee boxes preference?

indicators.note: to box something is to enclose it, so the words hold a run of letters inside

parts.note: the letters run through the end of the name and into the next word

explanation.surface: At Augusta, the golf course, a golfer picks their favourite tee box.
explanation.walkthrough: Augusta National hosts the Masters golf tournament, and a tee box is where golfers drive from, so 'boxes' looks like part of golf.
explanation.definitionFit: Taste can mean a liking or fondness for something, a personal preference, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Bishop exposes fights

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
to out someone is to expose their secret

explanation.surface: A bishop reveals the quarrels in his diocese.
explanation.walkthrough: B for bishop comes from chess notation; outs is the verb, exposing someone publicly.
explanation.definitionFit: A bout is a boxing or wrestling contest, so bouts are fights in a ring.

clue.text: Learner driver panics avoiding wide vehicles

parts.note: L is for learner, from the L-plate on a learner's car

indicators.note: avoiding something means keeping clear of it, so that letter is left out

parts.note: panics and worries are both fretting
W is the cricket abbreviation for a wide, a ball bowled out of reach

explanation.surface: A learner driver panics as they swerve to avoid wide trucks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wide vehicles' wants to be one phrase, but wide is the W to be dropped from WORRIES. Lorry is British for a truck.
explanation.definitionFit: Lorries are large goods trucks, the British word for heavy road haulage vehicles.

clue.text: Proclaim President Macron finally leaves hospital department

parts.note: Donald Trump, US president

indicators.note: something that leaves goes away, so that letter is taken out

parts.note: ENT is the ear, nose and throat department

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the word before it

parts.note: the final letter of this name

explanation.surface: President Macron is announced as finally leaving a hospital ward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'President Macron' reads as one name, but President alone is TRUMP; Macron just supplies the N that comes out of ENT.
explanation.definitionFit: To trumpet news is to announce it loudly and widely, as with a fanfare.

clue.text: Unusual street name in fashion

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: the rage is the current fashion
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: An odd street name is suddenly fashionable.
explanation.walkthrough: Something 'all the rage' is in fashion, which is why fashion gives RAGE; N goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Strange and unusual both describe what is odd, out of the ordinary or unfamiliar.

clue.text: Fancied gentleman's covered by legal document

indicators.note: something covered by another is wrapped around, so it goes inside

parts.note: a deed is a legal document, as for property
sir is the title for a gentleman

explanation.surface: A fancied gentleman is bound by a legal contract.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for is, joining the gentleman to the containment.
explanation.definitionFit: To fancy someone or something is informal for wanting it, so fancied means wanted or longed for.
